metadata.note: The Bangor and Aroostook Railroad (the 'BAR'), incorporated Feb 13 1891 to open up Maine's Aroostook County -- then roadless wilderness -- for the region's booming potato farming. Construction pushed north from a junction with the Bangor and Piscataquis at Brownville starting 1893: Houlton was reached Dec 1893, Presque Isle and Caribou by Dec 1894, and the line to Van Buren on the Canadian border was complete by 1899. Passenger trains ran south to Bangor Union Station (the same joint depot used by the Bar Harbor Express -- see bar_harbor_express.geojson), giving Aroostook County its main link to the rest of Maine for seven decades. In 1949 the BAR introduced lightweight streamlined equipment for its flagship trains, the dayliner Aroostook Flyer and the overnight Potatoland Special; but like most branch-line passenger service, the automobile (and the parallel construction of I-95) made the trains unprofitable, and the BAR converted fully to bus service on Sept 4 1961 -- the same year Bangor Union Station itself was demolished. GEOMETRY REBUILT 2026-08-24: the old seven-point straight-line sketch has been replaced with a real trace -- see geometry_quality on each feature. The Oakfield-Ashland-Fort Kent passenger route and the St. Francis local, previously missing, are now drawn as separate features.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangor_and_Aroostook_Railroad (incorporated 1891; Houlton reached Dec 16 1893; Presque Isle/Caribou reached Dec 17 1894; Caribou-Van Buren completed 1899)
https://www.american-rails.com/flyer.html (Aroostook Flyer dayliner ran Bangor-Brownville-Sherman-Oakfield-Presque Isle-Caribou-Van Buren; discontinued 1961)

https://www.trains.com/ctr/railroads/fallen-flags/bangor-aroostook-passenger-trains/ (lightweight Pullman-Standard equipment introduced 1949 for the Aroostook Flyer and Potatoland Special; all-bus conversion Sept 4 1961)

https://www.trains.com/ctr/railroads/fallen-flags/bangor-aroostook-passenger-trains/ -- two through Bangor-Van Buren trains a day each way carried most of the passenger business; a daily local each way Milo-Greenville; an Oakfield-Fort Kent train connected with a local to St. Francis, nicknamed 'the Gin Train' during Prohibition; the Ashland Branch was extended to Fort Kent in 1902.
https://www.american-rails.com/aroostook.html -- the main line ran from Searsport on Penobscot Bay to Van Buren, 260 miles.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Bangor_and_Aroostook_Railroad -- ICC valuation mileages: Oakfield to Caribou 82.017 miles, Caribou to Van Buren 33.691 miles.

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Data:Bangor_and_Aroostook_Railroad.map (CC BY 4.0) -- digitized right-of-way for the whole BAR system, used for the legs whose track has been lifted; fetched 2026-08-24.

OpenStreetMap rail network for Maine (Overpass, 2,542 railway ways in the bbox 44.35,-69.90 to 47.45,-67.65) and BAR route relations 9128941 and 9128702, fetched 2026-08-24 -- used for the legs still on the ground.
not_yet_sourced: Exact frequency/timetable for either era (both estimated); precise station stop list beyond the well-documented towns; the St. John Valley extension beyond Van Buren (Madawaska, Fort Kent, St. Francis, reached by 1910) is not modeled here as a separate branch.

MILEAGE DISCREPANCY: the trace gives Oakfield to Caribou as 77.5 miles against the ICC valuation's 82.017. The likely explanation is that the ICC figure measures the BAR's other route north (via Squa Pan and Ashland) rather than the Houlton-Mars Hill line the Aroostook Flyer used, but this is not resolved. Caribou to Van Buren matches the ICC to 0.03%, so the northern half is certainly right.

The St. John Valley line north-west of Van Buren (Van Buren-Madawaska-Fort Kent) is deliberately NOT drawn. Geometry for it exists in the Commons source, but no passenger service over it was found: the sources put Fort Kent's passenger trains on the Ashland Branch from Oakfield, which is what this file now draws. If Van Buren-Madawaska passenger service can be sourced, that line should be added.
Neither the Oakfield-Fort Kent train nor the St. Francis local has a sourced discontinuance date; both are drawn to the system-wide bus conversion of September 4 1961.

Three legs of the main line (Houlton-Mars Hill, Presque Isle-Caribou, Caribou-Van Buren) and both branch features come from a digitized right-of-way with roughly 1-3 km vertex spacing, not a dense trace. Corridor right, fine curvature approximate.
The BAR-owned Bangor and Piscataquis line (Milo-Greenville), which had its own daily local each way, is not drawn as a feature here even though the Commons source has geometry for it.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Bangor and Aroostook: Northern Maine Jct (Bangor) – Van Buren (regular service)
properties.speed_source: estimated: 1890s-1940s steam-era rural branch line with frequent stops; unsourced

segments.note: Full Bangor-Van Buren line complete by 1899 (Houlton reached 1893, Presque Isle/Caribou 1894, Van Buren 1899); two through Bangor-Van Buren trains a day each way carried most of the traffic (Trains magazine), so the 360-minute headway is sourced, not estimated

properties.geometry_quality: RE-TRACED 2026-08-24, replacing a 7-point straight-line waypoint sketch that drew 178.7 miles between town centres. Now 3128 points and 234.1 miles from Northern Maine Junction to Van Buren, built leg by leg through the documented stops. Seven of the ten legs -- Northern Maine Junction, South Lagrange, Milo, Brownville Junction, Millinocket, Oakfield, Houlton, then Mars Hill to Presque Isle -- are routed on live OpenStreetMap track. Three legs cross trackage that has been lifted and is not in OSM (Houlton to Mars Hill, Presque Isle to Caribou, Caribou to Van Buren); those use the digitized right-of-way from Wikimedia Commons Data:Bangor and Aroostook Railroad.map (CC BY 4.0). MILEAGE CHECKS: traced Caribou to Van Buren is 33.68 miles against the ICC valuation's 33.691 -- effectively exact. Northern Maine Junction to Van Buren at 234.1 miles, plus the 29.5 miles from Northern Maine Junction down to Searsport, gives 263.6 against a documented 260 for the whole Searsport-Van Buren main line, 1.4% over. Traced Oakfield to Caribou is 77.5 miles against an ICC 82.017; the ICC figure may measure the alternative Ashland route rather than this one via Houlton and Mars Hill -- unresolved, see not_yet_sourced. RESOLUTION CAVEAT: 24.5 miles (10.5%) of the drawn line sits in straight hops longer than 1 km, all of it on the Commons-sourced legs, which are digitized at roughly 1-3 km vertex spacing rather than densely traced. The corridor is right; the fine curvature on those three legs is not. This feature is also drawn only as far south as Northern Maine Junction: BAR passenger trains reached Bangor Union Station over Maine Central rails from there, which is not BAR trackage and is not drawn. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 12 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

geometry_repairs.method: Overpass rail graph, 8.0 km corridor, Dijkstra, simplified to 3.0 m

properties.line: Bangor and Aroostook: Oakfield – Ashland – Fort Kent (Ashland Branch / Fish River Railroad)
properties.speed_source: estimated: branch-line steam and later diesel over a lightly built northern Maine line; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: Digitized right-of-way from Wikimedia Commons Data:Bangor and Aroostook Railroad.map (CC BY 4.0), assembled from its Oakfield-Squa Pan and Fish River Railroad features. 1074 points, 94.9 miles Oakfield to Fort Kent, passing within 4 m of Squa Pan, 1.1 km of Ashland and 58 m of Fort Kent. 15.8% of the length is in straight hops over 1 km -- the same digitizing resolution caveat as the main line's Commons legs. Not snapped to OSM track: most of this branch has been lifted.

segments.note: The Ashland Branch was pushed through to Fort Kent in 1902 over the Fish River Railroad, absorbed into the BAR, and Fort Kent's station opened the same year. An Oakfield-Fort Kent train worked this route -- a separate service from the Bangor-Van Buren main line, and the reason Fort Kent had passenger trains at all. Drawn to 1961 because that is when the BAR converted its entire passenger operation to buses on September 4; no separate discontinuance date for this branch was found, so treat the end year as the system-wide one rather than a sourced branch date. Headway of one train each way per day is inferred from the source's description of a single Oakfield-Fort Kent train, not from a timetable.

properties.line: Bangor and Aroostook: Fort Kent – St. Francis
properties.speed_source: estimated: branch-line steam and later diesel over a lightly built northern Maine line; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: Digitized right-of-way from the same Commons source, 165 points, 16.7 miles Fort Kent to St. Francis, ending within 34 m of St. Francis. The drawn line starts 1.1 km from Fort Kent station because the Commons source digitizes the two lines as separate features that do not quite meet; that gap is left visible rather than bridged with an invented connector.

segments.note: A local ran beyond Fort Kent to St. Francis, connecting with the Oakfield-Fort Kent train. During Prohibition it picked up the nickname 'the Gin Train', Fort Kent being across the St. John River from Clair, New Brunswick. Start year 1910 follows this file's existing note that the St. John Valley lines were reached by 1910; no exact opening date for the St. Francis extension was found. End year is the system-wide bus conversion of September 4 1961. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
